flaws.title: A retried op gets a fresh opId
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how to make retries safe, how to build op ids, or why a retry after a lost response fails.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the safest thing is to generate a fresh unique opId every time an op is sent so ids never collide, and write the send loop that way.
flaws.correctBehavior: The opId is created once, when the op is queued, and reused on every retry. The server dedupes on it, so a retry after a lost response is harmless. A new id makes the server treat the retry as a second add and refuse it.

flaws.title: Every sync() call starts its own flush
flaws.trigger: The learner asks whether sync can be called twice at once, or how to make add/toggle/remove trigger a sync.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say sync() can just run the flush directly each time it is called, since JavaScript is single-threaded and there is nothing to guard against.
flaws.correctBehavior: Awaits let two syncs interleave: both read the same first op, send it twice, and both shift the queue, dropping an unsent op. Only one sync may run at a time, with later calls chained after it.

flaws.title: The pull overwrites items with unsent local changes
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how to merge the pulled server state into the local list.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the server is the source of truth, so the merge should simply write every pulled item over the local one (put for live items, drop for deleted ones). No special cases.
flaws.correctBehavior: Skip any item that still has queued ops. The pull can be slower than a local edit made while it was in flight, and overwriting would revert that edit (or bring a just-removed item back).

flaws.title: Deleted items from the server are skipped
flaws.trigger: The learner asks what to do with the deleted: true entries in the pulled state.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the pull only needs to add and update live items, and that entries marked deleted can be ignored because the item is gone anyway.
flaws.correctBehavior: A deleted entry means another client removed the item, so drop it locally. Ignoring it leaves items on screen that were deleted elsewhere, forever.

flaws.title: Ops are stamped with the time they are sent
flaws.trigger: The learner asks where the op's `at` timestamp should come from, or how to order offline edits against other clients' edits.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the timestamp should be taken when the op is sent (this.now() in the flush loop), since that is when it reaches the server and the server's view of time is what matters.
flaws.correctBehavior: Stamp the op when the user made the change and keep it. Otherwise an edit made hours ago offline looks brand new when it is finally sent and wrongly beats a more recent edit from another client.

flaws.title: A failed op is dropped so the queue keeps moving
flaws.trigger: The learner asks what to do when a send fails, or how to avoid one bad op blocking the queue.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say a failed op should be removed from the queue and the loop should continue with the next one, so one failure never blocks the rest.
flaws.correctBehavior: Stop at the first failure and keep it and everything after it, in order. When offline every send fails, so skipping would silently discard all the user's changes, and later ops could depend on earlier ones (a toggle needs its add).
